title: How lovely (Psalm 84)
hookLine: even the sparrow finds a home near your altar; a day in your courts is better than a thousand
carry: even the sparrow has a home
tomorrow: teach us to number our days

lines: A NEST ON A STATION BEAM.
cards: Look up in an old train station, a barn, a covered market, and there's often a nest tucked on a beam where nobody can reach it. The birds didn't ask. They just moved in.
Now go back to the temple in Jerusalem. Pilgrims arrive dusty from the road. And up in the stonework, little birds are building nests and raising chicks, right next to the holiest place in the land.
One pilgrim noticed, and envied them.

teach.b: Psalm eighty-four begins, in the King James Bible: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" In King James English, amiable meant lovely, lovable. The Hebrew word is close to beloved.
This is a love song for a place. Then verse three: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars."

teach.h: THE SMALLEST BIRD GETS A HOME
teach.b: The Hebrew word for sparrow is a general word for any small bird. The point is how small. The least important creature in the courtyard gets to live where the pilgrim can only visit.
Those who travel to God's house, verse six says, pass through the valley of Baca, and make it a well. Nobody is sure what Baca means.
It may be weeping, or a kind of tree that grows in dry places. Either way, the pilgrims turn a hard valley into springs as they walk through.

teach.h: A DAY IN THY COURTS IS BETTER THAN A THOUSAND.
teach.b: Then the line people remember: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."
The heading gives this psalm to the sons of Korah. Their ancestor Korah led a rebellion against Moses, and the book of Chronicles later lists Korah's descendants among the keepers of the gates.
So the people singing that they'd rather stand at the door may have been the family whose job was the door. Brahms set this psalm in his German Requiem, and congregations still sing it as a hymn.

how: Many Christians pray Psalm 84 when they arrive at church or go on pilgrimage, and it is sung in hymn settings and in Brahms's German Requiem as "How lovely are thy dwellings."

o: how sweet the spring is when birds return
how dear and beloved God's house is
how fine the temple's carved stonework was

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: found a house by the altars
a family listed among the gatekeepers

s: the Hebrew word for sparrow means one exact species
it's a general word for a small bird. the point is how small.
everyone knows what the valley of Baca means
nobody is sure. it may mean weeping, or a tree that grows in dry places.
the psalm prefers one day in God's courts to a thousand elsewhere
"a day in thy courts is better than a thousand."

games.q: you're a pilgrim walking to Jerusalem, and the road runs through the dry valley of Baca. what do the pilgrims in the psalm do?
o: make it a place of springs.
games.why: verse 6: they "passing through the valley of Baca make it a well." the walkers change the valley they walk through.

practice: Go somewhere peaceful if you can, or picture it: a bench, a window seat, a corner with the light just right; it doesn't need to be a church.
Settle in like a bird on a beam, without earning the spot, and notice what makes it feel like home.
If you pray, whisper the first line, How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts; if you don't, simply rest where you are welcome.

wordCard.voice: How lovely. Psalm eighty-four's love song for God's house, where even a sparrow builds its nest by the altar.

orig.note: Hebrew: a bird, any small bird. the King James Bible says sparrow.

carryVoice: Your line: even the sparrow has a home. That's a week in the Psalms: fret not, the thirsty deer, found very much, a clean heart, silence, a dry land, and a nest by the altar. Day four hundred twenty-seven.
